body.en: A *company* is an artificial person created by law (the Companies Act, 2013), with a separate legal entity: it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name. Its capital is divided into shares; shareholders have limited liability (only up to the unpaid amount on their shares). It has perpetual succession: its existence is not affected by the death or exit of members. It acts through a common seal or authorised signatories and is managed by a board of directors elected by shareholders, so ownership and management are separate. Shares of a public company are freely transferable.

body.en: Forming a company passes through stages. Promotion: the idea is conceived, its feasibility studied, the name approved, and the Memorandum of Association (the charter: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital) and Articles of Association (internal rules) drafted. Incorporation: documents are filed with the Registrar of Companies, who issues a Certificate of Incorporation, after which the company exists as a legal person. A public company then raises capital (prospectus, allotment of shares) and begins business after the legal requirements for commencement are met. Merits: large capital, limited liability, continuity, professional management. Limitations: complex *formation*, lack of secrecy, delays, and conflicts between owners and managers.

problem.en: Why is a company said to have perpetual succession? Explain with an example.

steps.en: A company is a separate legal person, distinct from its members.
Its existence does not depend on who its members are.
Shares may be transferred, and members may die or leave, but the company continues.
Example: the founders of an old company have long died, but it still exists and does business.

answer.en: Its life is independent of its members; only a legal process can end it.
